A breakdown of Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) tailored for finance leaders and business founders, comparing how COGS is calculated in Consumer Packaged Goods (CPG) versus Software as a Service (SaaS) business models. Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Provides a clear, foundational understanding of how COGS and Gross Margins differ between CPG and SaaS businesses, including common accounting misclassifications that distort valuations. modules: [FIN] topics: [COGS, SaaS accounting, CPG accounting, gross margin, financial valuation, unit economics, AWS server costs, freight classification] tier: 3 scope_hint: baseline

Topics. unit economics / how COGS determines the remaining capital available for marketing and R&D per unit sold; valuation / why venture capitalists and private equity firms obsess over gross margin (which is dictated by COGS) when valuing a business; CPG COGS / calculating tangible COGS using raw materials, direct labor on the manufacturing floor, factory overhead, freight-in, and packaging; SaaS COGS / calculating intangible COGS using server costs (AWS/Azure), third-party delivery APIs, customer support wages, and onboarding/implementation wages; accounting flow / how CPG inventory hits the balance sheet as an asset before flowing to the P&L as COGS upon sale, whereas many SaaS costs (like wages) hit the P&L immediately; gross margin expectations / expecting 20-40% gross margins for manufacturing/CPG versus 70-90% for SaaS; freight misclassification / the common accounting error of recording "freight-out" (shipping to customers) as COGS, when it should be recorded as a selling/operating expense; SaaS misclassifications / incorrectly recording Customer Success wages (which are sales/upsell functions) or third-party revenue shares as COGS instead of operating expenses.

The Freight Classification Rule: The strict accounting rule that "freight-in" (bringing materials to the factory) is part of COGS, but "freight-out" (shipping the final product to the customer) is an operating/selling expense and should NOT be in COGS.

The Customer Success Misclassification: Noting that while Customer Support and Implementation wages belong in SaaS COGS, Customer Success teams (who handle upsells and renewals) are a sales function and belong in operating expenses.
Gross Margin Benchmarks: The rule of thumb that traditional CPG/manufacturing businesses operate at 20-40% gross margins, whereas SaaS businesses operate at 70-90% gross margins.

SaaS Server Depreciation: The explanation that if a company owns its physical servers, the cost enters COGS as depreciation over time, but most modern companies rent via AWS/Azure and log the monthly fee directly as COGS.
